title: App Development with User Stories
summary: How real apps get made: the types of app and the roles in an app team, writing user stories with acceptance criteria and prioritising them, wireframing screens and flows, building with event-driven programming and data, testing with a proper test plan, and launching, measuring and improving an app ethically using agile sprints.
learn: The types of app and the roles in an app development team
How to write user stories with acceptance criteria and prioritise them
How to design app screens and navigation with wireframes
How apps use events, variables and stored data
How to test an app with a test plan and report bugs
How agile teams launch, measure and improve apps ethically
intro: There are millions of apps, but the good ones all start the same way: with a real person and a real need. In this topic you'll work like a professional app team. You'll learn how apps are built and who builds them, turn users' needs into user stories, design screens with wireframes, build features with event-driven code, test them properly, and plan how to launch and improve your app without tricking users. By the end you'll have planned (and maybe built) an app of your own.

pages.title: How apps are made
pages.spec: Describe types of app, the roles in an app development team and the stages of app development
pages.summary: Apps can be native (built for one platform), web apps (run in a browser) or cross-platform. Professional apps are made by teams including product managers, designers, developers and testers. Most teams use agile methods, building and improving apps in short cycles called sprints.
pages.starter: Name an app you use every day. How many people do you think it took to make it?
sc: I can compare native, web and cross-platform apps
I can describe roles in an app development team
I can describe the agile approach to app development

b: Native app: built for one platform (iOS or Android), downloaded from an app store
Web app: runs in a browser; works on any device
Cross-platform: one codebase that runs on both iOS and Android
Each has trade-offs in speed, cost and features
Product manager: decides what to build and why
UX/UI designer: designs how it works and looks
Developers: write the code (front end and back end)
Testers: find bugs; data analysts: measure how it's used
Build in short cycles called sprints (often 1-2 weeks)
Each sprint delivers a small working improvement
Get feedback from users, then adapt
The opposite of planning everything up front ("waterfall")

blocks.text: Types of app

blocks.caption: Types of app
head: Type
What it is
Advantages
Disadvantages
rows: Built for one platform, e.g. Swift for iOS, Kotlin for Android
Fast; full access to phone features
Must build twice for iOS and Android
Works on any device; no download
Less access to phone features; needs internet (usually)
One codebase built for both iOS and Android

blocks.text: The app team

blocks.title: Roles in an app team
items: Product manager: understands users and the business, and decides priorities
UX/UI designer: researches users, designs layouts, flows and visuals
Front-end developer: builds what users see and interact with
Back-end developer: builds the servers, databases and APIs behind the app
Tester (QA): plans and runs tests to find bugs
Data analyst: studies how people use the app

blocks.text: Small start-ups may have one person doing several jobs; big apps have hundreds of people. AI coding assistants now help developers write code faster, but people still decide what to build and check that it works.
Agile development

**[[agile|Agile]]** is an approach where teams build software in short cycles called **[[sprint|sprints]]**, often one or two weeks long. Each sprint delivers a small, working improvement that users can try. The team gets feedback and adapts the plan. This contrasts with the **waterfall** approach, where everything is planned up front and the product is delivered at the end.

blocks.caption: Agile vs waterfall
head: Feature
Agile
Waterfall
rows: A little at a time; plan changes

blocks.title: App autopsy
steps: Choose an app you know well (e.g. a messaging, music or school app).
Decide whether it's native, web or cross-platform (or find out).
List the team roles that would have been needed to build it.
Describe one improvement you think was delivered in a recent update, and how an agile team might have decided on it.

q.q: Which roles would be needed for your app, and what would each do?
q.a: E.g. for a music app: product manager decides on new features like shared playlists; designer designs the playlist screens; front-end developers build them; back-end developers store playlists and stream music; testers check it works on different phones; data analysts see how many people use it.

q.q: How might an agile team have decided on a recent update?
q.a: E.g. analytics showed users struggled to find downloads, so the next sprint added a "Downloads" tab, released it to some users first, and checked whether they used it more.

check.q: What is a native app?
o: An app built for one specific platform
An app made in a jungle

check.q: Which type of app runs in a web browser?
What is a sprint in agile?
o: A short cycle that delivers a small working improvement

check.q: Who decides what an app team builds next and why?

practice.a: Native built for one platform/downloaded from store (1); web app runs in a browser on any device (1); native faster/more phone features but must build for each platform (1).

practice.q: Explain one advantage of agile development.
practice.a: Frequent feedback from users (1) so the team can adapt/fix problems early/deliver value sooner (1).

pages.title: User stories and priorities
pages.spec: Write user stories with acceptance criteria and prioritise them using MoSCoW and a product backlog
pages.summary: User stories describe what a user needs and why: "As a ..., I want ..., so that ...". Acceptance criteria list the conditions that show a story is done. Teams keep stories in a product backlog and prioritise them, for example using MoSCoW: Must, Should, Could, Won't (this time).
pages.starter: You're making an app for the school canteen. What do pupils, canteen staff and parents each want from it?
sc: I can write user stories in the correct format
I can write clear acceptance criteria
I can prioritise user stories using MoSCoW

b: As a [type of user], I want [goal], so that [reason]
Focus on the user's need, not the technology
Different users have different stories
e.g. "As a pupil, I want to see today's menu, so that I can decide whether to bring lunch"
Conditions that must be true for the story to be "done"
Specific and testable
Often written as Given ... When ... Then ...
e.g. Given it's a school day, when I open the app, then I see today's menu with prices
Product backlog: the list of all stories, in priority order
MoSCoW: Must have, Should have, Could have, Won't have (this time)
MVP: the minimum viable product, the smallest version that's useful
Build the Musts first, release, learn, then add more

blocks.text: User stories
A **[[user story]]** describes a feature from the user's point of view:
**As a** [type of user], **I want** [a goal], **so that** [a reason].
The "so that" part is important: it explains why the feature matters, helping the team find the best solution.

blocks.caption: User story examples for a school canteen app
head: User
Story
rows: As a pupil, I want to see today's menu, so that I can decide whether to bring a packed lunch.
As a pupil with a nut allergy, I want to see allergy information for each meal, so that I can eat safely.
As a parent, I want to top up my child's account, so that they don't run out of money.
As the canteen manager, I want to see how many people pre-order each meal, so that I can reduce food waste.

blocks.text: Acceptance criteria

**[[acceptance criteria|Acceptance criteria]]** are the conditions that must be met for a user story to count as done. They must be specific and testable. Many teams write them as **Given ... When ... Then ...**

blocks.title: Acceptance criteria for the allergy story
blocks.context: As a pupil with a nut allergy, I want to see allergy information for each meal, so that I can eat safely.
steps: Given I'm viewing the menu, when I tap a meal, then I see a list of the 14 major allergens it contains.
Given a meal contains nuts, when I view the menu, then it shows a clear allergy warning icon.
Given I've set my allergy in my profile, when a meal contains that allergen, then it is highlighted in red.
blocks.answer: Each criterion can be tested with a clear pass or fail, so the team knows exactly when the story is done.

blocks.text: Prioritising: backlog and MoSCoW
The **[[product backlog]]** is the team's list of all user stories, in priority order. Teams can't build everything at once, so they prioritise using **[[MoSCoW]]**:

blocks.caption: MoSCoW prioritisation
head: Priority
Meaning
Canteen app example
rows: Essential: the app fails without it
Important but not essential for the first version

blocks.text: A **[[minimum viable product]]** (MVP) is the simplest version of an app that's still useful to real users, usually just the Must haves. Teams release the MVP, learn from users and then add more.

blocks.title: Story workshop
steps: Choose an app idea: a homework planner, a school club finder, or a local bus times app for Fermanagh.
Identify three types of user and write at least six user stories.
Write acceptance criteria (Given ... When ... Then ...) for two of your stories.
Prioritise all stories with MoSCoW and circle your MVP.

q.q: Write two user stories for different users.
q.a: E.g. homework planner: "As a Year 8 pupil, I want to see all my homework deadlines in one list, so that I don't miss any." "As a parent, I want a weekly summary of my child's homework, so that I can support them."

q.q: Write acceptance criteria for one story.
q.a: E.g. Given I've added homework with a due date, when I open the app, then it appears in a list sorted by due date; Given homework is due tomorrow, when I open the app, then it's highlighted in orange.

check.q: What is the correct format for a user story?
o: As a ..., I want ..., so that ...

check.q: What are acceptance criteria?
o: Testable conditions that show a story is done

check.q: What does the M in MoSCoW stand for?
What is an MVP?
o: The simplest version of an app that's still useful

practice.q: Write a user story for a pupil using a school sports club app.
practice.a: Correct format "As a ..., I want ..., so that ..." (1); sensible goal and reason (1).

practice.q: Explain why teams prioritise user stories using MoSCoW.
practice.a: Can't build everything at once/limited time (1); ensures essential features built first (1); can release an MVP sooner and learn from users (1).

pages.title: Wireframes and flows
pages.spec: Design app screens and navigation using wireframes, user flows and common mobile UI patterns
pages.summary: Before coding, designers sketch screens as wireframes, simple layouts showing where content and buttons go. User flows show the steps a user takes to complete a task. Designers use familiar UI patterns, design mobile-first and follow accessibility guidelines so apps are easy for everyone to use.
pages.starter: Draw your phone's home screen from memory in 60 seconds. What did you include?
sc: I can create a low-fidelity wireframe
I can draw a user flow for a task
I can apply common UI patterns and accessibility guidelines

b: A simple sketch of a screen's layout
Boxes for images, lines for text, labelled buttons
Low-fidelity: quick pencil sketches; high-fidelity: detailed mock-ups
Focus on layout and function, not colours
The steps a user takes to complete a task
Start → screens and decisions → goal reached
Fewer steps usually means a better experience
Each user story becomes a flow
Familiar patterns: bottom tab bar, search bar, cards, back button
Mobile-first: design for small screens, then scale up
Touch targets big enough for fingers
Good contrast, readable text, labels for screen readers

blocks.text: Wireframes

A **[[wireframe]]** is a simple drawing of a screen's layout, showing where content, images and buttons go. It deliberately ignores colours and styling so the team can focus on structure and function.

blocks.caption: Wireframe fidelity
head: Type
What it looks like
When to use
rows: Quick pencil sketches with boxes and labels
Detailed mock-ups with real colours, text and images
Final design before building; testing with users

blocks.text: User flows

A **[[user flow]]** is a diagram of the steps a user takes to complete a task, from start to goal, including screens and decisions. Every user story can become a flow. Good design usually means fewer steps.

blocks.title: User flow for "top up my child's canteen account"
steps: Home screen → tap "Top up".
Choose child (if more than one) → choose amount (£5, £10, £20 or other).
Confirm payment with fingerprint → see "Success" and new balance.
blocks.answer: Four screens and one decision. The designer might remove a step by remembering the last child and amount used.

blocks.text: UI patterns
A **[[UI pattern]]** is a common design solution that users already understand. Using familiar patterns means people don't need to learn your app from scratch.

blocks.title: Common mobile UI patterns
items: Bottom tab bar: 3-5 main sections, always visible
Search bar at the top
Cards: boxes that group information about one item
Back arrow in the top-left corner
Pull down to refresh; swipe to delete
Floating action button for the main action (e.g. "+ Add homework")

blocks.text: Mobile-first and accessible
**[[mobile-first|Mobile-first]]** design means designing for small phone screens first, then adapting for tablets and computers. Accessibility guidelines include:

items: **[[touch target|Touch targets]]** at least about 44-48 pixels so they're easy to tap
High contrast between text and background
Text that can be resized
Labels on buttons and images so screen readers can describe them
Not relying on colour alone to show meaning

blocks.title: Wireframe sprint
steps: Using your app idea from last lesson, choose your three Must-have user stories.
Draw a user flow for one of them.
Sketch low-fidelity wireframes for each screen in that flow (use the phone templates).
Swap with another pair and test: can they complete the task by "tapping" your paper screens? Note any confusion.

q.q: Draw or describe your user flow.
q.a: E.g. homework planner, "add homework": Home → tap "+" → enter subject, task and due date → tap "Save" → back to Home with the new item in the list.

q.q: What confused your testers, and what will you change?
q.a: E.g. "They didn't notice the + button at the bottom, so we'll make it larger and add a label 'Add homework'."

check.q: What is a wireframe?
o: A simple sketch of a screen's layout

check.q: What does a user flow show?
o: The steps a user takes to complete a task

check.q: Which is a common mobile UI pattern?
o: A button smaller than a pinhead
A hidden menu with no icon

check.q: What does mobile-first mean?

practice.q: Explain why designers create wireframes before coding.
practice.a: Quick/cheap to change ideas (1); agree layout and test with users before spending time coding (1).

practice.q: Describe three ways to make an app's screens more accessible.
practice.a: Any three: large touch targets (1); high contrast (1); resizable text (1); screen reader labels (1); don't rely on colour alone (1).

pages.title: Building with events and data
pages.spec: Explain event-driven programming and how apps use variables, lists, stored data and APIs
pages.summary: Apps are event-driven: code runs when events happen, such as a button tap, a timer or a new message. Apps use variables and lists to hold data while running, and store data on the device or in a cloud database so it's kept. Many apps get live data from other services through APIs.
pages.starter: When you tap "Send" in a messaging app, what do you think the code has to do?
sc: I can explain how apps store data locally and in the cloud
I can explain how apps use APIs

b: An event is something that happens: a tap, a swipe, a timer, a message arriving
An event handler is the code that runs when that event happens
"When Save button clicked → do this"
The app waits for events, then responds
Variables: store single values (score, username)
Lists: store many values (homework items)
Local storage: on the device; works offline
Cloud database: shared, synced across devices
Apps request data or services from other systems
Weather, maps, payments, login with Google
The app sends a request; the API sends back data (often JSON)
Saves building everything yourself

blocks.text: Event-driven programming

Most apps use **[[event-driven programming]]**. An **[[event]]** is something that happens: a button tap, a swipe, typing, a timer going off, a location change, or a message arriving. An **[[event handler]]** is the code that runs when that event happens. The app spends most of its time waiting for events.

blocks.title: Event handler for adding homework (pseudocode)
blocks.context: A homework planner has a text box, a date picker and a Save button.
steps: WHEN SaveButton.Clicked:
IF TaskBox.Text is empty THEN show "Please enter a task"
ELSE add {task, subject, due date} to homeworkList, save the list, clear the boxes, refresh the screen
blocks.answer: The code only runs when the Save button is clicked (the event), and validates input before saving.

blocks.text: Variables, lists and storage

items: A **[[variable]]** stores a single value while the app is running, such as a username or score.
A list stores many values, such as all homework items.
Data in variables is lost when the app closes, so apps save data to storage.

blocks.caption: Where apps store data
head: Storage
Where
Good for
rows: Sharing between users, syncing across devices, backups

blocks.text: A school canteen app would need a cloud database so that the canteen, pupils and parents all see the same menu and balances.
APIs

An **[[API]]** lets an app request data or services from another system. Instead of building everything themselves, developers use APIs for weather, maps, payments, translation, AI features and "Sign in with Google". The app sends a request, and the API sends back data, often in a format called JSON.

Tools such as MIT App Inventor and Thunkable let you build real phone apps with blocks, including events, lists, databases and APIs. AI app builders can now generate apps from a description, but you still need to understand events and data to check and fix what they produce.

blocks.title: Event mapping
steps: For your app, list five events users or the system could trigger (e.g. tap Save, swipe to delete, 8am timer).
For each event, write what the event handler should do in pseudocode, including input checks.
Decide what data your app stores: which variables, which lists, local or cloud, and why.
Identify one API your app could use. If you have time, build one screen in App Inventor or Thunkable.

q.q: Write the event handler for one event.
q.a: E.g. WHEN 8am timer fires: FOR each homework item IF due date = today THEN send notification "Due today: [task]".

q.q: Should your app store data locally or in the cloud? Explain.
q.a: E.g. homework planner: cloud, so homework syncs between phone and school laptop and isn't lost if the phone breaks; but settings can stay local.

check.q: What is an event?
o: Something that happens, like a tap or timer

check.q: What is an event handler?
o: Code that runs when an event happens

check.q: Why do apps save data to storage?
o: Data in variables is lost when the app closes

check.q: Which storage lets data sync across a user's devices?

practice.q: Explain what is meant by event-driven programming.
practice.a: Code runs in response to events (1), e.g. button taps/timers/messages (1).

practice.q: Explain why a homework app might use a cloud database rather than local storage.
practice.a: Data syncs across devices (1); backed up if phone lost/broken (1); could be shared with teachers/parents (1).

pages.title: Testing and bugs
pages.spec: Plan and carry out testing using a test plan with normal, boundary and erroneous data, and write useful bug reports
pages.summary: Testing checks that an app works as intended and meets its acceptance criteria. A test plan lists tests, the data used and expected results. Good testing uses normal, boundary and erroneous data, tests on different devices, and includes beta testing with real users. Bugs are recorded in clear bug reports.
pages.starter: What's the most annoying bug you've found in an app or game? How do you think it got through?
sc: I can write a test plan with expected results
I can choose normal, boundary and erroneous test data
I can write a clear bug report

b: Bugs annoy users, lose data and can create security holes
Testing checks the app meets its acceptance criteria
Test as you go, not just at the end
Test on different devices, screen sizes and connections
Normal: sensible data that should work (age 13)
Boundary: at the edges of what's allowed (age 11 and 18)
Erroneous: data that should be rejected (age "cat" or -5)
Each test has an expected result
Bug report: title, steps to reproduce, expected vs actual, device, screenshot
Severity: how bad is it?
Beta testing: real users try the app before the full release
AI-written code needs testing too

blocks.text: Test plans
A **[[test plan]]** lists what will be tested, the test data, the expected result and (after testing) the actual result.
Boundary tests are important because programmers often make mistakes with < and <=. Erroneous tests check the app copes with bad input rather than crashing.
Testing on real devices

blocks.title: What else to test
items: Different phones, screen sizes and operating system versions
Slow or no internet connection
Accessibility: screen readers, large text, colour contrast
Security: can one user see another user's data?
Every acceptance criterion from the user stories

blocks.text: Bug reports
A **[[bug report]]** tells developers exactly how to find and fix a problem.

blocks.caption: A good bug report
head: Part
Example
rows: App crashes when saving homework with an emoji in the title
Homework is saved and shown in the list
High: users lose what they typed

blocks.text: Beta testing

**[[beta testing|Beta testing]]** means releasing an almost-finished app to a group of real users before the full launch. They find bugs and usability problems the team missed. App stores provide tools for beta testing.
Code written with help from an AI assistant can look correct but contain bugs or security problems. It needs exactly the same careful testing as code written by a person.

blocks.title: Break it!
steps: Your teacher shares a simple (deliberately buggy) app or web form, e.g. a club sign-up form.
Write a test plan with at least eight tests, including normal, boundary and erroneous data.
Run the tests and record the actual results.
Write two bug reports for the most serious bugs you found.

q.q: Give one boundary test and one erroneous test from your plan.
q.a: E.g. club sign-up for Years 8-10: boundary: Year 10, expected accepted; just outside boundary: Year 11, expected rejected; erroneous: "ten", expected rejected with a helpful message.

q.q: Write one of your bug reports.
q.a: Title: Form accepts a blank email. Steps: 1. Fill in name and year. 2. Leave email blank. 3. Press Submit. Expected: error "Please enter your email". Actual: form submits with no email. Device: school Chromebook. Severity: Medium.

check.q: What is boundary data?
o: Data at the edges of what's allowed

check.q: What is erroneous data?
check.why: Wrong type or out of range.

check.q: Which part of a bug report helps developers recreate the problem?
What is beta testing?
o: Real users trying an almost-finished app before launch

practice.q: An app accepts a quantity from 1 to 10. Give one normal, one boundary and one erroneous test value.
practice.a: Normal, e.g. 5 (1); boundary, e.g. 1 or 10 (or 0/11 just outside) (1); erroneous, e.g. "abc" or -3 (1).

practice.q: Explain why apps should be tested on different devices.
practice.a: Screens/OS versions/hardware differ (1), so layouts or features may break on some devices (1).

pages.title: Launch, measure, improve
pages.spec: Describe how apps are launched, measured and improved, and evaluate ethical issues including privacy and dark patterns
pages.summary: Launching an app involves app store review, a privacy policy and clear descriptions. After launch, teams use analytics and user feedback to decide what to improve in the next sprint. Apps make money through prices, subscriptions, adverts or in-app purchases. Ethical apps respect privacy and avoid dark patterns that manipulate users.
pages.starter: Have you ever felt tricked into tapping something in an app? What happened?
sc: I can describe how apps are published and maintained
I can explain how analytics and feedback drive improvements
I can identify dark patterns and design ethical alternatives

b: App stores review apps for safety, privacy and quality
A privacy policy must explain what data is collected
Clear description, screenshots and age rating
Plan for updates: bugs, new OS versions, security
Analytics: how many users, which features, where they quit
Feedback: reviews, surveys, support messages
A/B testing: show two versions to different users and compare
Each sprint: pick the most valuable improvements from the backlog
Business models: paid, subscription, ads, in-app purchases
Dark patterns trick users: hidden costs, hard-to-cancel subscriptions, fake countdowns
Ethical design: honest choices, easy to cancel, privacy by default
Children's apps must follow the UK Children's Code

blocks.text: Launching an app
To publish on the Apple App Store or Google Play, developers submit their app for **[[app store review]]**, where it's checked for safety, privacy, content and quality. Apps need:

items: A clear description, screenshots and an age rating
A **[[privacy policy]]** explaining what data is collected, why, and who it's shared with
Privacy labels summarising data use

blocks.text: After launch, apps need maintenance: fixing bugs, updating for new phone operating systems and patching security problems.
Measuring and improving

**[[analytics|Analytics]]** tools record how people use an app: how many users there are, which features they use, how long they stay and where they give up. Combined with reviews and feedback, this helps the team decide what to build in the next sprint.
**[[A/B testing]]** shows two versions of a feature to different groups of users and measures which works better.

blocks.title: An A/B test
blocks.context: The homework app wants more pupils to add homework on the day it's set.
steps: Group A sees the normal home screen.
Group B sees a reminder at 4pm: "Got any homework today? Tap to add it."
After two weeks, 40% of group A and 62% of group B added homework on the day it was set.
blocks.answer: Version B works better, so the team rolls it out to everyone, as long as users can turn the reminder off.

blocks.text: Making money

blocks.caption: App business models
head: Model
How it works
Watch out for
rows: Pressure to spend, especially in games

blocks.text: Dark patterns
A **[[dark pattern]]** is a design trick that pushes users into doing something they didn't intend.

blocks.caption: Dark patterns and ethical alternatives
head: Dark pattern
Example
Ethical alternative
rows: "No thanks, I don't like saving money"
Easy to subscribe, very hard to cancel
Cancel in as few steps as signing up
"Only 2 left! Offer ends in 05:00" when it isn't true
Extra fees revealed at the last step
Show the full price up front
Repeated pop-ups asking for permissions or ratings
Ask once, at a sensible time
Confusing settings that make you share more

blocks.text: In the UK, the Children's Code (Age Appropriate Design Code) requires apps likely to be used by children to have high privacy settings by default, collect minimal data and avoid "nudge" techniques that encourage children to give up privacy.

blocks.title: Launch plan
steps: For your app, write the app store description, age rating and three privacy label points.
Choose a business model and explain why it's fair to your users.
Choose three analytics measures you'll track and one A/B test you'll run.
Check your design for dark patterns using the table, and fix any you find.

q.q: Which business model did you choose, and why is it fair?
q.a: E.g. free with an optional £1.99 one-off "pro" upgrade for themes; no ads or data selling, so pupils' data stays private; the core features stay free.

q.q: Describe one A/B test you'll run.
q.a: E.g. test two versions of the "add homework" button (a floating "+" vs a labelled button) and measure which leads more users to add homework in their first week.

check.q: What does app store review check?
What is A/B testing?
o: Comparing two versions with different groups of users

check.q: What is a dark pattern?
o: A design trick that pushes users into doing something they didn't intend

check.q: What does the UK Children's Code require?
o: High privacy settings by default for children's apps

practice.q: Explain how analytics help an app team decide what to improve.
practice.a: Shows how users use the app/where they give up (1); team prioritises fixes/features with most impact (1).

practice.q: Evaluate the use of in-app purchases in games aimed at young people.
practice.a: Benefits, e.g. free to try, pay only for what you want, funds developers (1-2); concerns, e.g. pressure, dark patterns, overspending, loot boxes (1-2); conclusion (1). Max 4.
